issue_context.title: Pdf document with image displayed in low quality
comments: > What went wrong? (add screenshot) In https://mozilla.github.io/pdf.js/web/viewer.html logo image is rendered in low quality compared to Firefox rendering > > ![exampleInViewer](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84440240/231173865-10cb29d4-674f-4685-a373-4be118a4a24d.png) Does it work also better if you open your PDF document with https://mozilla.github.io/pdf.js/web/viewer.html *in Mozilla Firefox* instead? If so, this is likely a bug in Google Chrome rather than the PDF.js library; please keep in mind that Firefox is the primary development target here. > > What went wrong? (add screenshot) In https://mozilla.github.io/pdf.js/web/viewer.html logo image is rendered in low quality compared to Firefox rendering > > ![exampleInViewer](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84440240/231173865-10cb29d4-674f-4685-a373-4be118a4a24d.png) > > Does it work also better if you open your PDF document with https://mozilla.github.io/pdf.js/web/viewer.html _in Mozilla Firefox_ instead? If so, this is likely a bug in Google Chrome rather than the PDF.js library; please keep in mind that Firefox is the primary development target here. You are right when I opened PDF document with https://mozilla.github.io/pdf.js/web/viewer.html in Mozilla Firefox everything looks good, probably this is the Google Chrome issues I'm not sure. But I also use the 'pdf-dist' library in my app in both browsers (Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox). I tried different versions of the library and noticed that this problem appears starting from version 2.11.338. I investigated the changes that were made in version 2.11.338. Perhaps the change https://github.com/mozilla/pdf.js/commit/f38fb42b42b7ba9e6f421fbd88a337a371d81ccd in which function "getImageSmoothingEnabled" (..\src\display\canvas.js) was added, led to this problem. I debugged the 'pdfjs-dist' code and found that for my pdf image, the value 'interpolate' = false, so then the value 'fillCtx.imageSmoothingEnabled' is set to false. If I set the value 'fillCtx.imageSmoothingEnabled' to true then my image in pdf document looks good. ![1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84440240/231422996-173c3cf0-755f-40e8-a535-84bd4dddc2f1.png) Maybe you can add a global option like force image smoothing? > Maybe you can add a global option like force image smoothing? Sorry, but we simply can't add options for everything that users may want. Please keep in mind that every new option adds code/maintenance/support overhead, since having a bunch of mostly unused and completely untested options often causes problems later on.[1] Given that it works in Firefox, which is the primary development target, the recommendation would be to file a (canvas-related) bug against Google Chrome and/or add the needed option in your own fork of the PDF.js library. --- [1] Please note that over the last couple of years we've actually tried to *remove* rarely used functionality/options, in order to simplify maintenance. Hey! @Snuffleupagus , I and @nicolo-ribaudo did some research around this issue, and we think it can be resolved if PDF.js would "always" smoothen the image while downscaling, maybe by reversing the if, else-if [here](https://github.com/mozilla/pdf.js/blob/master/src/display/canvas.js#L924-L929). This change doesn't change the current behaviour of pdf.js in FireFox, since firefox always smoothens the images when downscaling. The [isDownScaling check](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/3c194fa1d6f339036d2ec9516bd310c6ad612859/dom/canvas/CanvasRenderingContext2D.cpp#4933) in Firefox was added in https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1360415 (for pdf.js) following an [HTML change](https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/5854cb07f075e5219df8ad645370bb2818cf5a62) that explicitly decided to allow engines to always do interpolation for downscaling. The chrome's internal PDF viewer (along with other readers like Adobe acrobat, macOS built-in, edge built-in), ignores the interpolate property of the image and always smoothens it while downscaling. But since there's no downscaling check in chrome itself, it causes the pdf.js viewer to not smoothen the images, resulting in the blurry PDFs. Here's the screenshots from different viewers for the same PDF: PDF.js viewer in chrome: Chrome Built-in viewer: MacOS built-in viewer: Safari built-in viewer:

review_comments:
I'm not entirely sure why, but this change does still seem to affect Firefox looking at the reference test results, and given this comment and the linked bug I would not expect any changes in Firefox. Notice how on the `firefox-bug956965-page33` tests seems to be more "blocky" now (also for Chrome by the way).

I went over all other changed tests and all of them seem like an improvement, so this particular one isn't a blocker for me, but I figured I'd ask since I can't really explain this change.

It's because here we're considering that we downscale when the scale factor is lower than deviceRatio x 96/72 when in Firefox it's when the factor is lower than 1.
So we're taking into account the resolution.
And about `firefox-bug956965-page33`, I was surprised too but in checking on a non-hdpi screen (an old one I got almost 10y ago), there is no perceptible differences.
Thank you for the explanation; in that case this sounds good to me and doesn't require further changes.

Shouldn't this be `||` instead of `&&` like before? I would think that if only one of the dimensions is reduced we would still need to apply smoothing, but on the other hand I'm not sure if it's even possible for only one of them to change without the other one changing as well, so I might be mistaken here...

Good question, I asked me the same.
And I think that we've an upscale when only one dimension is upscaled and I think in this case we must respect the value of the flag.
That said in Firefox it's a &&:
https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/3c194fa1d6f339036d2ec9516bd310c6ad612859/dom/canvas/CanvasRenderingContext2D.cpp#4927-4928

OK, let's indeed keep this logic in sync with what Firefox does. In that case, however, we should probably also change `<=` to `<` given that we shouldn't need to smoothen when the dimensions are exactly equal, only when we have to downscale.
If one dimension is equal and the other one is downscaled it should still smoothen, right?

Hm, I think you're right. That does make me wonder about the Firefox code though, and brings me back to the initial question of using `||` , so I guess I'm just not entirely sure what would be correct here. Considering that the reference tests didn't show many changes with the current version of the patch I'm not too worried about regressions here, so I'm also fine with keeping the current logic and adapting it later on if need be (because in that case we'll also have a test case that triggers the behavior).
